result.summary: Bellerophon, exiled for a killing, is purified by Proetus but falsely accused by Stheneboea. Sent to Iobates with a letter ordering his death, he kills the Chimera on Pegasus, defeats the Solymi, Amazons and Lycian ambushers, and wins Iobates' daughter and kingdom.

scenes.title: Slander at the court of Proetus
scenes.summary: Bellerophon is purified by Proetus. Stheneboea falsely accuses him after he rejects her, and Proetus sends him off with a letter ordering his death.
scenes.stakes: Bellerophon risks death through a false accusation and a sealed order for his execution.

scenes.title: Iobates sets the Chimera task
scenes.summary: Iobates reads the letter and sends Bellerophon against the Chimera, a three-headed fire-breathing beast whose parentage is variously told.
scenes.stakes: Bellerophon faces a beast stronger than many men.

scenes.title: Trials and triumph in Lycia
scenes.summary: Bellerophon kills the Chimera from Pegasus, then defeats the Solymi, the Amazons and the Lycian ambushers. Iobates shows him the letter, gives him Philonoe and leaves him the kingdom.
scenes.stakes: Bellerophon must survive a series of tasks meant to kill him.

alias_notes.explanation: Variant tradition names the brother Piren or Alcimenes.

notable_quotes.reason: Describes the Chimera's composite form and the plan to destroy Bellerophon with it.

analysis.text: A false accusation sends a hero on a series of lethal tasks, each of which he survives, so the plot against him turns into his rise to a kingdom.
Apollodorus records competing versions of names and parentage, showing the Library's habit of collecting variant traditions.

legacy.text: The letter ordering the bearer's death gave rise to the phrase 'Bellerophontic letter' for a message carried unknowingly to one's own doom.
The Chimera gave English the word 'chimera' for a fanciful or impossible idea.

fun_facts.text: Homer mentions the Chimera and the sealed letter in the Iliad, Book 6.

language_notes.text: Variant names for the brother killed reflect competing traditions; the compiler simply lists them rather than choosing one.
"Purified": ritually cleansed of the pollution of bloodshed, required before a killer could be received socially and religiously.
"Vicious proposal": she claims he tried to seduce her, reversing what actually happened.
"More than a match for many": stronger than many men together, so sending one man seemed certain death.
Homer (Iliad 16) says the Chimera was reared by Amisodarus; Hesiod (Theogony) makes it the offspring of Typhon and Echidna, monstrous parents.
The Solymi were a warlike people of the Lycian region, neighbours of Lycia.

context_notes.text: Proetus, wary of violating guest-right by killing Bellerophon himself, sends him to Iobates, Stheneboea's father, carrying the sealed message.
Pegasus, the winged horse, sprang from Medusa's neck when Perseus beheaded her; Poseidon was his father.
The Amazons were a legendary nation of women warriors.

literary_notes.text: Bellerophon unknowingly carries his own death warrant, trusting the king who sends him.
The Chimera is a composite monster of lion, goat and dragon, emphasizing its unnatural, overwhelming danger.
The intended victim ends as king: the letter meant to destroy him becomes the proof of his triumph.
